title: Stapleton's fourth proposition: freedom from deadly sins
source_text: XLIII. Cap. 5. Docet mandatorum impletionem in hac vita talem non esse ut omni prorsus peccato careat: tamen talem & tantam esse ut gravibus illis & lethiferis peccatis omnino carere possit & debeat. Justos quidem ipsos etiam interdum lethaliter peccare: Verum in tali peccato constitutos justos non esse, neque legem implere: nec veram justitiam cum tali peccato, nondum per poenitentiam deleto, consistere, licet cum aliis levioribus peccatis, etiam quotidie commissis, vera hujus vitae justitia consistat.
pass_a_gloss: XLIII. Chap. 5. He teaches that the fulfilment of the commandments in this life is not such that it is wholly free from all sin: yet that it is such & so great that it can & ought to be wholly free from those grave & deadly sins. That the just themselves indeed sometimes sin mortally: But that those set in such sin are not just, nor fulfil the law: nor does true righteousness stand with such a sin, not yet blotted out by repentance, although the true righteousness of this life stands with other lighter sins, even those committed daily.
pass_b_english: Thesis XLIII. In chapter 5 he teaches that in this life the fulfilment of the commandments is not such as to be entirely free of all sin, but that it is such, and so great, that it can and must be entirely free of grave and deadly sins.

The righteous themselves, he grants, sometimes sin mortally. But while they are in such a sin they are not righteous and do not fulfil the law, and true righteousness cannot coexist with such a sin until repentance has blotted it out. The true righteousness of this life does coexist, however, with other, lighter sins, even those committed every day.

lemmas.gloss: it is wholly free from all sin
not yet blotted out by repentance

choices.why: Thomas Stapleton, whose twelve books on justification Le Blanc summarizes as a Roman witness to the imperfection of the obedience of the justified.
